agree.reason: The partners committing to three days, the long notice, the commuting money and the plain admission that this changes the terms people were hired on will bring most staff along, but the eleven remote hires outside the far-away group get nothing beyond $150 and a review with no stated criteria, so some will push back or leave.

honest.reason: The 30% figure is carefully hedged, but saying the clients' comment "cost us both projects" and describing the team as "people who didn't work together day to day" go further than what the clients actually said.

works_the_facts.reason: The figures are repeated rather than worked: the draft never says that 15 of 46 is a third of the firm, and it leaves out the strongest fact available, that 5 of the 6 project leads already come in three days a week on their own.

right_comparison.reason: The draft never spells out what happens if nothing changes, such as more lost finals or juniors continuing to take 30% longer to lead projects, so readers have no concrete picture of the status quo to weigh the change against.

qualification.reason: The March 2028 review has a date, but it names nothing to be measured, no threshold, and no outcome that could change the policy, and the hedge on cause gives readers nothing they could check.

objections.reason: It deals directly with the broken-terms objection and the desk shortage, but it doesn't speak to remote hires who live just under two hours away, and it doesn't say whether the six-month review could actually loosen the rule.

fit.reason: It is a one-page email with a clear subject line and sensible headings, and it ends with the Friday 10 a.m. meeting details and who to contact beforehand, as the brief asked.
